I would have immediately told the people, by means of the radio and the newspapers, you will not receive any more cheques for that amount before six months.
Some may say that a* family of ten would get $1,000 and a family of twenty, $2,000. But there can never be more than thirty-six people in one family.
Distribution would be general for the benefit of every Canadian. People would be encouraged to work and to produce more. I would tell them that during the next six months no new money will be issued, that they will earn their wages as usual, without anybody being socialized, and that at the end of that period, if they have produced more, they will be given more. If they have produced much, they will receive much. If they cease producing and there be more money than products, money surpluses will have to be taxed where they lie. They will have to be taxed if there is too much money in circulation for the available goods. This would be in the interest of our people. In this way, employees and workers would be encouraged to work and to produce more. We have the example of the subsidies which were granted during the war to encourage production. When they were removed, prices went up. Consumers could not buy as much as before and producers had to produce less because of a curtailed demand. Therefore I suggest that subsidies should be continued while controls should be removed in this country. The Minister of Finance, as well as the hon. members opposite, claim that to distribute the sum of $100 to each Canadian citizen would be sheer folly. Parliament has

The Budget-Mr. Caouette

the power and the duty to assume control of the issue of money and credit in the country and to distribute them fairly in order to help all our citizens and to provide them with the security and the freedom which would be theirs if purchasing power were based upon the tremendous possibilities of Canada. Mr. Speaker, my hon. friends have voted themselves an additional 82,000 last year; did this increase in their indemnities make them any lazier than they were last year?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we wish to ward off communism, it is time the members of this house united their efforts in fighting the rise of communism in this country. In order to do so, it is time we struck a balance of this country's assets and liabilities, we determined the profits earned by the work of organized society and distributed new money to all members of that society who shared in the economic and social activities which led to Canada's vast production, a society which represents the great physical producing power of our country.
Mr. Speaker, were everyone in this house to contribute toward giving the Canadian people that guarantee, toward giving

Canada to the Canadians, toward using Canadian money and production to the advantage of the citizens of our country, I could warrant that communism would never win any ground here, because our people would be happy and fully satisfied, knowing that Canada would henceforth be theirs and realizing how grand it is to live in such a wealthy country as ours, in a country that needs no one from outside to dictate to it. Let us be worthy of our responsibilities. We are all responsible to the Canadian electors and not to a party. Our duty demands that we deprive the financial magnates of their power to control and that we place the assets of the country at the service of the Canadian people.

speechtext:
After listening and catching the odd word, I am sure that some of us have regrets at not having a real knowledge of French so that we could; understand the oratory and enthusiasm to which we have just listened. However, I still see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) delivering his budget. He stood up; he spoke up; he had something that he was extremely proud of, and then he sat down. If other hon. members did the same thing we would not have the urgent need for improvement in our acoustics.
I had some regrets when I heard the budget. I thought the luxury taxes would be eliminated. I had not understood thoroughly the reductions that had been made. Of course, to me jewellery and jewellery stores should not be taxed as luxuries because they sell things which are absolutely necessary to the home life of Canada. Take clocks and watches and wedding rings. Anybody would admit that the use of a wedding ring is necessary for the upbuilding of a good home. I congratulate the minister on the announcement which appears in the press today that $17,500 will be proposed in the supplementary estimates for the support of the Olympic games. I think it is in keeping with good Liberal policies, and it is telling the youth of Canada that they should keep fit physically and mentally. I am sure that when the Olympic games are on and our own flag rolls up high, when our lady from Ottawa, Miss Barbara Ann Scott, takes part, whether she wins or not, we shall be extremely proud of her.
This brings to mind one of the outstanding needs of the House of Commons-and it is not loud speakers that I am going to speak about. The outstanding need of the House of Commons is, first, a good gymnasium and, second, a good swimming pool. When we

The Budget-Mr. Mclvor
come here and the session opens we are in fit physical shape, but we have to do so much sitting around that we do not get our physical exercise or our setting up exercises unless we do them in our own rooms. I can see men putting on fat. Hon. members will agree that fat is a dead weight, and doctors will tell us that it is a tug on the heart; therefore we should have a good gymnasium. I hope that when Ottawa is beautified we shall have this institution to help to beautify the human body.
I should like to make some reference to the provinces. Perhaps somebody with more weight and intelligence could deal with this matter better than I, but I am going to deal with it in my own way. I look on Canada, the land of my adoption, as a big family. A properly regulated Christian family has authority somewhere. It should be in the father; sometimes it is in the mother, but it is usually in a combination of both, since they are one. The family of Canada should not have its authority in British Columbia; it should not have it in Quebec; it should not have it in Ontario; it should have it here in Ottawa. There should be an authority that Canada will be proud of. I do not think we would be very proud of our cabinet ministers if they went so far as to change the constitution of Canada to the detriment of our country. I hope that there will be no breakdown in that regard. I am thinking of the song that is sometimes sung here, "The more we are together, the happier we will be."
I should like to congratulate the minister in that he did not forget old age pensions. In that respect he supported what was contained in the speech from the throne. Some people outside the house thought there would be an increase in old age pensions. If the pension is increased to S30 I hope that every province in Canada will add as much as British Columbia has added to it, and therefore there will be a decent pension for our old age pensioners. As I said before, if the Liberal government is left long enough in power I expect that one day the old age pension will be $50 a month.
I should like to speak of the pensioners of the first great war. I have congratulated the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) behind his back on the work that he, his committee and1 the government have done in looking after the pensioners of the recent war, but I find that pensioners of the first war need some consideration. I have had delegations call on me, and I had sense enough not to promise more than I was sure of. I had one 83166-1831
group of men tell me of a pensioner who was getting a 100 per cent pension, and this is what I found. He pays $33 a month rent; groceries, $30; coal, $10, and that does not heat the house very well; meat, $12; milk $9; bread, $2.50; light and telephone, $7.50, making a total of $104. All he gets is $100, and his rent is to be raised $5 a month because of the change in the rental regulations. The same amounts I have given do not include anything extra for medicine; they do not include anything for clothes for himself or his wife. They do not include anything for insurance or the odd bottle of ginger ale, and I think the Minister of Veterans Affairs will give more consideration to these pensioners. I have advocated before that employees on railways and elsewhere should have a national pension sponsored by a central authority in the dominion government. It should be contributory, because, as we know men who earn good1 salaries are inclined to spend their money as they receive it and they are nearly always broke the first week after they get their pay. But if a man is compelled to contribute to a pension fund he will have something in his old age. Alternatively, he should be compelled to put his money into annuities.
In Fort William there are two things that we would like the government to pay a little more attention to. Our hospitalls are in straitened circumstances. When I think of our hospital and what it is doing for the dominion government, I suggest that we should have more consideration in connection with the building of the new McKellar hospital wing. I am informed by our hospital board that fifteen beds are necessary at all times for veterans and1 Indians. I will not say more about that just now, but I think some attention should be given to it.
When I spoke before in the house I mentioned an outstanding need in northwestern Ontario and west of Fort William, and that is that some consideration be given to the distress under which gold miners are trying to do their work. We have in the Shebandowan district a splendid place for operations in gold mining and we think some relief should be given. We have these resources that are perhaps second to none in all Canada.
Some reference was made this afternoon to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). A good deal was said, and then I thought of the farmers in my own district and the benefit they have derived from the experimental substation there. I can remember when I bought eggs at fifteen cents a dozen by the case, but farmers do not have to sell eggs at that figure today. They are better off and are better sat-
The Budget-Mr. Mclvor

isfied than they have, ever been, and1 we hope that we shall not find it necessary to go back to the old way of doing things.
When I think of the reduction in taxation proposed in this budget, and how it affects me, I can see that it will give me a little more money to spend, and if there is anything I like to do it is to spend money that is my own, so that the more I get in the form of a reduction in taxes, the more I shall have to spend. I think, therefore, that what is given in the budget in this way comes in very handy.
I am sorry that the children cannot get their chocolate bars and soft drinks, but I am informed by a doctor of dentistry that this is not so bad because it is a splendid thing for children's teeth when they do not have so much sugar. I know from my experience as a boy that the more candy you eat, the oftener you have to go to the dentist.
When I think of the reduction in taxes I think of a donkey we had on the farm at one time. If you twisted his tail something was bound to happen and you would not be standing there when it did. But if you twisted the donkey's tail the donkey would be there just the same. You did not change the donkey. Well, you can find fault with this budget all you like, but the reduction it makes is a splendid thing and' I congratulate the minister.
